title: Gemini API Managed Agents: 3.6 Flash, hooks, and more
gist: Google DeepMind upgraded Gemini API Managed Agents: Gemini 3.6 Flash becomes the silent default on the antigravity-preview-05-2026 agent, environment hooks let customer scripts block, lint or audit every tool call inside the remote sandbox, and new max_total_tokens budget caps, cron triggers, an Environments API and free-tier access turn agents into scheduled, cost-capped workers. AI-native investment bank OffDeal is cited running post_tool_execution hooks to verify 30+ deck logos with Gemini vision before they reach a banker-ready deck.

themes.theme: Flash-class models as the agentic default

insights.claim: Google has silently switched the antigravity-preview-05-2026 managed agent to Gemini 3.6 Flash as its default model, with no code changes required and the swap taking effect on the developer's next interaction.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Silent default upgrades mean live agent behaviour and cost per task can change without a deploy — a real operational risk for anyone running production agents on hosted APIs.
insights.quote: The antigravity-preview-05-2026 agent now runs Gemini 3.6 Flash by default. No code changes are required.
insights.locator: Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default

insights.claim: The supported model list for managed agents is entirely Flash-class — Gemini 3.6 Flash (balanced default), Gemini 3.5 Flash (previous generation) and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (lowest latency and cost) — with no Pro tier offered for autonomous agent loops.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads are being served by cheap high-throughput models, not flagship ones; that compresses revenue per token but multiplies token volume — the key variable for inference-capex payback math.

insights.claim: Developers can pin a specific model by passing agent_config.model, which is the only defence against Google rotating the default underneath a running workload.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Model pinning discipline is becoming a due-diligence question for any company whose product economics depend on a hosted model's cost and behaviour.
insights.locator: You can also explicitly select models by passing agent_config.model

insights.claim: Gemini API managed agents now support environment hooks: a .agents/hooks.json file makes the runtime execute custom scripts on pre_tool_execution or post_tool_execution events around every tool call the agent makes inside its sandbox.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Deterministic pre/post-execution control is the missing enterprise requirement for autonomous agents; shipping it inside the hosted runtime pulls governance work away from third-party agent-ops vendors.
insights.locator: Environment hooks: block, lint, and audit tool calls

insights.claim: A denying hook does not just block the action: when the script returns {"decision": "deny", "reason": "..."} the tool call is skipped and the rejection reason is injected into the model's context, turning policy enforcement into a steering signal the agent can react to.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Feeding denial reasons back into context is how policy layers become self-correcting rather than merely obstructive — a design pattern to look for when evaluating agent-governance products.
insights.quote: If the script returns {"decision": "deny", "reason": "..."}, the tool call is skipped and the rejection reason is passed into the model’s context.

insights.claim: Hook matchers accept regular expressions, so a single rule can target several tools with | or intercept every tool call with *, and hooks also support an http handler type that POSTs to an external endpoint.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: HTTP handlers let existing enterprise policy engines and SIEM stacks sit outside the sandbox and still gate agent actions — lowering the integration barrier for regulated buyers.
insights.locator: The matcher field supports regular expressions

themes.theme: OffDeal as production proof in financial services

insights.claim: OffDeal, described as an AI-native investment bank, runs an AI analyst called Archie and uses post_tool_execution hooks to run an automated image-verification pipeline inside Google's remote sandbox.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: A named financial-services customer running agents in production is evidence the agent stack is crossing from demo to revenue workflow in a high-compliance vertical.
insights.locator: Teams are already using hooks to build production-grade validation pipelines.

insights.claim: The blocker before hooks was structural, not model quality: because the managed sandbox is remote, customer validation code had nowhere to execute, which prevented OffDeal from using Gemini's managed agents at all for this workload.
insights.speaker: Alston Lin, Founder & CTO of OffDeal
insights.so_what: Adoption of hosted agent platforms is gated by the ability to run proprietary validation code next to the agent — a checklist item to test when assessing any managed-agent vendor.
insights.quote: Before agent hooks, we couldn’t do this on Gemini’s managed agents: the sandbox is remote, so our validation code had nowhere to run.
insights.locator: OffDeal is an AI-native investment bank

insights.claim: OffDeal's quality bar illustrates why raw generation is insufficient for banker deliverables: a single deck can need 30+ company logos each verified for correct company, size, aspect ratio, embedded name, transparent background and contrast on white.
insights.speaker: Alston Lin, Founder & CTO of OffDeal
insights.so_what: The moat in vertical AI is the deterministic verification wrapper around the model, not the model itself — where defensible margin accrues in AI-native services firms.
insights.quote: often 30+ logos in a single deck, every one of which must be the right company, the appropriate size and aspect ratio, contain the name, have a transparent background, and have a high contrast when placed on a white slide.
insights.locator: OffDeal is an AI-native investment bank

insights.claim: OffDeal's hook fires the instant Archie writes its company list, fetching candidate logos, enforcing pixel-level checks, verifying each one with Gemini vision, and publishing a manifest of approved files that are the only images allowed into the deck.
insights.speaker: Alston Lin, Founder & CTO of OffDeal
insights.so_what: Model-checks-model plus an allowlist manifest is a replicable architecture for making probabilistic agents safe for client-facing output — worth benchmarking any vertical-AI startup against.
insights.locator: With hooks, a post_tool_execution hook triggers our pipeline

themes.theme: Budget controls and agent unit economics

insights.claim: Google concedes that multi-turn autonomous agent loops can consume significant token budgets, and has added a max_total_tokens cap in agent_config covering input, output and thinking tokens together.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Explicitly counting thinking tokens against the cap confirms reasoning tokens are billable and are the main runaway-cost vector in agentic workloads — the line item to model when forecasting AI COGS.
insights.quote: you can pass max_total_tokens inside agent_config to cap total consumption (input + output + thinking)

insights.claim: Hitting the token cap pauses execution and returns status "incomplete" with environment state preserved, so work can be resumed via previous_interaction_id with a fresh budget rather than restarted.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Checkpointed budgets make cost caps safe to set aggressively, which removes a key blocker to enterprises letting agents run unattended.
insights.quote: execution safely pauses and the interaction returns status: "incomplete"
insights.locator: When the agent reaches the limit

insights.claim: Managed agents are now available on free tier projects, so developers can run agentic workflows with an API key from a project that has no active billing attached.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Giving away sandboxed compute-heavy agent runs is an expensive top-of-funnel land grab — a sign Google is prioritising developer share over near-term margin in the agent platform race.
insights.quote: Managed agents are now available on free tier projects.

insights.claim: Scheduled triggers bind an agent, environment, prompt and cron schedule into a persistent resource that fires without human intervention, with each run reusing the same sandbox so files persist between executions.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Cron-driven stateful agents shift consumption from bursty human-initiated chat to always-on machine demand — structurally the most bullish pattern for sustained inference volume.
insights.quote: A trigger binds an agent, environment, prompt, and cron schedule into a persistent resource that fires without manual intervention. Each run reuses the same sandbox, so files persist across executions.

insights.claim: A new Environments API lets developers list, inspect and delete sandbox sessions programmatically, recover environment IDs after a disconnect, and clean up rather than wait out the default 7-day sandbox TTL.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: A 7-day default TTL means idle sandboxes are a real cost and state-management surface; sandbox lifecycle is becoming a cloud-resource category of its own.
insights.quote: clean up sandboxes when your pipeline finishes instead of waiting for the 7-day TTL.

insights.claim: In the Gemini Interactions API a single API call coordinates reasoning, code execution, package installation, file management and web retrieval inside an isolated cloud sandbox, collapsing what is normally a multi-component orchestration stack into one hosted primitive.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: Google absorbing orchestration into the model API compresses the addressable market for standalone agent-framework and orchestration startups.
insights.quote: a single API call coordinates, reasoning, code execution, package installation, file management, and web retrieval inside an isolated cloud sandbox
insights.locator: With managed agents in the Gemini Interactions API

insights.claim: Google closes by positioning managed agents as "cost-controlled, scheduled workers" that run autonomously in real development environments "without breaking your budget or requiring external orchestration" — an explicit competitive shot at third-party orchestration layers.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: The stated positioning tells you where Google intends to compete next; assume orchestration vendors' differentiation window is closing.
insights.quote: without breaking your budget or requiring external orchestration

insights.claim: Google is distributing its own API documentation as an installable skill for coding assistants, instructing developers to run npx skills add google-gemini/gemini-skills --skill gemini-interactions-api so their AI assistant can use the Interactions API directly.
insights.speaker: Philipp Schmid
insights.so_what: When the buyer of API docs is another AI agent, developer-platform marketing shifts to being indexable by assistants — a new and cheap distribution channel to watch across API vendors.
insights.locator: If you're using an AI coding assistant
